# Do GitHub Pages Support PHP?

You will receive a `405 Method Not Allowed` error from GitHub Pages if you attempt to submit a form using PHP. This isn't a misconfiguration on your end or a bug in your code; it is a fundamental architectural limitation of the hosting platform. GitHub Pages serves static content only. It runs on a simplified version of Nginx that does not include the PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager) module required to parse and execute server-side scripts.

When you deploy a `gh-pages` branch, the CI/CD pipeline or the deployment process builds your site into a directory structure containing HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images. Once deployed, the server treats every file extension strictly as static data. When a browser requests a `.php` file, the server does not invoke an interpreter. Instead, it attempts to serve the raw source code as plain text or returns a `405` error if the request method (like POST from a form) conflicts with the static nature of the resource.

### The Static-Only Architecture

To understand why this happens, you have to look at how GitHub Pages handles requests. The platform is designed for documentation, portfolios, and marketing sitesâessentially anything that can be rendered by a browser without backend logic. The underlying infrastructure strips out the ability to run server-side languages like PHP, Python, or Ruby.

If you inspect the response headers or check the error logs on GitHub's side (which are not publicly accessible), you will see that the environment lacks the PHP-CGI binary. Even if you correct all syntax errors in your `index.php` and ensure your database credentials are valid, the server will never execute the code. It simply cannot.

### Why Not Just Use a Custom Domain with Apache?

A common workaround suggested in older forums is to point a custom domain to the GitHub Pages URL and use an external web server like Apache or Nginx running on a separate VPS to handle the PHP logic, while GitHub Pages handles the HTML. However, this approach creates a fragmented architecture that defeats the purpose of using a static site generator or the free hosting tier.

In this setup, your form submission would need to be proxied through an external API or require a backend service to process the data before returning a response to the frontend. This adds complexity and latency. It is also important to note that simply changing your DNS records to point a custom domain at `github.io` does not magically enable PHP processing on GitHub's servers. The code remains static regardless of the domain name pointing to it.

### Recommended Alternatives for Form Handling

Since server-side processing is unavailable, you must shift the logic to the client side or use third-party services that provide backend functionality without requiring you to manage a server.

1.  **Client-Side Validation and APIs**: Move form validation entirely to JavaScript using frameworks like jQuery Validation or modern libraries like Alpine.js or Vue. For data persistence, send the form payload to a public API (such as Formspree, EmailJS, or Web3Forms) via an AJAX request. These services handle the email delivery and logic on their end.
2.  **Static Site Generators with Plugins**: If you are building your site using a static site generator like Jekyll or Hugo, ensure your build process does not accidentally include PHP files in the public directory. The output directory should strictly contain `.html`, `.css`, and `.js` assets.
3.  **Laravel for Backend Logic**: If your application requires complex backend logic, session management, or database interactions, you should migrate that portion to a dynamic framework like Laravel. You can host the Laravel application on a standard VPS or a platform like Heroku, Render, or Fly.io, while keeping your static assets on GitHub Pages if needed. This separation of concerns ensures that PHP runs where it belongsâon a server capable of executing it.

### Moving Forward

The error message `405 not allowed` is the system telling you exactly what is missing: the ability to execute scripts. Accept this limitation and refactor your stack to use static technologies or external APIs. When you do deploy to a live production environment with full server capabilities, remember that the solution will work there because that environment will be configured with the necessary PHP modules and database connections.

For developers looking for robust dynamic applications that require full-stack capabilities right from the start, platforms like Laravel provide a comprehensive framework that handles routing, security, and database management out of the box. For more information on building secure, scalable web applications with modern stacks, you might explore resources available at [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com).
